## Upgrading from v0.6.0

**An `fc-*` birthmark that would be empty is no longer refused.** `extract`
returns it and warns instead, so a program that genuinely calls nothing gets a
birthmark, and one call-less file in a corpus no longer stops the extraction of
every file after it.

`Error::NoCallOperations` and `Error::UnresolvedCalls` are gone with the
refusals they reported. Code matching on them will not compile; there is
nothing to match, because nothing fails there any more.

**`Error::NoFunctionsLifted` is new**, so an exhaustive `match` over `Error`
needs one more arm. It belongs with `UnreadableOutput`: both say a lifter
reported success over output that cannot be used, and no argument the caller
could have given would change either.

## Highlights

- **A lift that found no functions is refused, not reported as a success.**
  `lift` read its output back and accepted a file with an empty `functions`
  array, so every birthmark taken from it was empty -- and two empty
  birthmarks score 1.0, which reports unrelated programs as identical. Nothing
  downstream could tell that apart from a lift that worked.

  It is not hypothetical. A Ghidra without its decompiler native binary
  produces exactly this: `DecompInterface` fails for every function, the
  lifting script skips each one, and `analyzeHeadless` exits 0 regardless.
  That happened on two platforms during this release and was noticed only
  because a test wanted a particular function name and found no names at all.

  For `ghidra-pcode` the message names that cause and the command that fixes
  it. The other representations get the fact without the advice: nothing has
  been measured about why they would come back empty, and a guess would send
  the reader to a Ghidra directory they do not have.

  A refusal rather than a warning, which is the opposite of the call made for
  an empty `fc-*` family in this same release. That one is a measurement -- a
  program that calls nothing genuinely calls nothing, and the family simply
  does not distinguish it. This is not: a binary worth comparing has
  functions, and every time oinkie has written a file without any, the tool
  was misconfigured rather than the binary unusual.

  `Error::NoFunctionsLifted` is new. It is a sibling of
  `Error::UnreadableOutput` rather than a case of it, because the two send the
  reader to different places: that file cannot be read, this one reads
  perfectly and says nothing.

- **`oinkie stats` summarises a set of birthmarks** (#129). Describing a
  dataset in a paper meant writing a script against the JSON each time; the
  command reports, for each group of birthmarks sharing an intermediate
  representation and a type, how many files there are, how many functions
  each holds, and how many elements each function's birthmark has — with min,
  quartiles, max, mean and standard deviation — plus the empty functions, the
  distinct elements, and for the `freq` shapes the total of the counts.
  `--per-file` adds a row per file and `--top N` the most frequent elements.
  It writes Markdown, CSV or JSON.

  Two counts that were both called "length" are kept apart by name:
  **functions** are the entries in a birthmark file, and **elements** are the
  items in one function's birthmark. The birthmark length is the second, which
  is also the sense #128's threshold uses, so this is the evidence for choosing
  one. The library's `Elements` type still names a function; #131 is about
  that.

  A file that does not read as a birthmark is skipped with a warning and
  counted in the output, so a summary never covers fewer files than it was
  given without saying so. A path that does not exist is an error, not a skip.

  `Kgram::ops` is new in the library, so a k-gram's operations can be read
  without going through serde.

- **An empty `fc-*` birthmark is a measurement, not a failure.** A program that
  calls nothing is a program that calls nothing, and the family simply does not
  distinguish it. Refusing was the tool deciding, on the caller's behalf, that
  the question could not be asked.

  What the refusal was really guarding was a lifter bug: an empty family is
  usually `is_call` recognising none of its own opcodes, and the symptom is
  indistinguishable from the legitimate result. That reasoning was right and is
  kept — as a warning that says which of the two cases it found, names the file
  and the representation, and leaves the reading to whoever asked. Both cases
  were reached by a real lifter during v0.6.0.

  The refusal also cost more than it looked: it was an `Err`, so a corpus with
  a single call-less binary in it lost every birthmark after that one.

- Dependencies updated. 66 packages moved within the ranges the manifest
  already declared, and two moved past them: `itertools` 0.14 to 0.15 and
  `num-derive` 0.4 to 0.5. Neither needed a line of code changed.

  `sha2` 0.10 to 0.11 is the third. Its `Output` no longer implements
  `LowerHex`, so `format!("{:x}", hash)` had to be written out — six lines, no
  new dependency, and the hashes it produces are unchanged, so no birthmark
  changes its filename. It renders only the bytes the prefix needs, where
  before it formatted all thirty-two and took sixteen characters.

  `ndarray` 0.17 is the one that could not move, and not for want of trying.
  `lapjv` takes the cost matrix for the Hungarian aggregator and requires
  `ndarray ^0.16`, so passing it a 0.17 array is a type mismatch — the same
  crate at two incompatible versions in one call. `lapjv` 0.3.0 is its latest
  and dates from September 2025.

  Replacing `lapjv` was measured rather than assumed. `pathfinding`'s
  `kuhn_munkres_min` is the only maintained alternative that does not itself
  depend on `ndarray`, and on random matrices it is 1.6 to 3.5 times slower —
  223 ms against 79 ms at n=2000 — and uses more memory, 155 MB against 93 MB.
  It also cannot take the similarities as they are: its weights must implement
  `Ord`, so `f64` has to be scaled to integers and rounded. Slower, larger, and
  less precise; `lapjv` stays, and `ndarray` stays at 0.16 with it.

  `rmcp` went 3.2.0 to 3.5.0 inside its existing range, which is the MCP server
  itself. A compiling server is not a working one, so `verify_mcp.sh` spoke the
  protocol to the built binary and read five tools back.

- **Ghidra lifts on Windows.** `lift -r ghidra-pcode` named
  `support/analyzeHeadless`, the bash script, so a Windows installation that
  had Ghidra reported it as missing. The Windows entry point is
  `support/analyzeHeadless.bat`, a public release carries both, and
  `std::process::Command` runs a `.bat` by substituting `cmd.exe` itself -- so
  the fix is the file's name and nothing else.

  Of the three platforms this is the one that needs the least: an official
  release ships prebuilt native binaries for Windows x86-64 and Windows ARM64,
  where macOS gets none and has to build its own.

  The test suite now runs whole on all three runners. Windows used to be given
  a list of the test binaries that hold no Ghidra test, and there is no list
  any more.

  Which spelling is used is decided by a `cfg!(windows)` at the call site
  rather than inside the function that answers it, so both can be asserted
  from either platform. A branch compiled away is a branch nothing reads, and
  that is how one spelling came to be the only one.

  Where Ghidra is looked for when `GHIDRA_HOME` is unset is now empty on
  Windows rather than three Unix paths -- as it is for IDA and Binary Ninja,
  whose candidates are macOS bundles. A path spelled for another operating
  system cannot be found, and only makes the message advise something
  impossible; `--home` and the environment variable are the route there, and
  the message now says so and stops.

- **The crates.io upload authenticates by trusted publishing.** crates.io
  recognises this repository and this workflow and issues a token that lives for
  the length of the job, so there is no long-lived secret here to leak, to
  rotate, or to forget to rotate.

  The `crates-io` job used to skip when `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` was unset, so
  that adding the job published nothing by itself. There is no such secret now
  and no such skip: a release that cannot authenticate fails, because the
  alternative is a tagged release with no crate and nothing saying so.

  The first upload could not have worked this way -- crates.io cannot scope a
  token to a crate that does not exist yet -- so 0.6.0 went out by hand.
